verdict.rationale: Three converging lexical (word-meaning based) strands ground the verdict. First, the intoxication-state vocabulary is uniformly condemned across the canon. In Hebrew, 'to be drunk' (shakar, H7937) and 'drunkard' (shikkor, H7910) appear with 'strong drink' (shekar, H7941) and 'wine' (yayin, H3196) in woe oracles (Isaiah 5:11,22; Habakkuk 2:15), wisdom warnings (Proverbs 20:1; 23:29-35), priestly restriction (Leviticus 10:9), and Nazirite separation (Numbers 6:3). In Greek, 'drunkenness' (methe, G3178) and 'revelry' (komos, G2970) are paired in vice lists (Galatians 5:21; Romans 13:13; 1 Peter 4:3), and Ephesians 5:18 issues a direct present imperative (an ongoing command) 'do not be drunk' (me methyskesthe, G3182), tagging the state as 'reckless dissipation' (asotia, G0810); 'drunkard' (methusos, G3183) is named in the 1 Corinthians 6:10 kingdom-exclusion catalog. Second, the positive sobriety word group ('be sober' (nepho, G3525) with 'be sound-minded' (sophroneo, G4993), 'temperate' (nephalios, G3524), 'self-control' (egkrateia, G1466) as fruit of the Spirit in Galatians 5:23 and 2 Peter 1:6) commands clear governed faculties as a standing obligation, making deliberate self-intoxication its lexical opposite. Third, Romans 13:1-2 attaches 'judgment' (krima, G2917) to resisting appointed 'authority' (exousia, G1849), engaging the illegal-drug clause. The principal disputed term is the pharmak- group: 'drug-mixing or sorcery' (pharmakeia, G5331, 2 occurrences) and 'drug-mixer or sorcerer' (pharmakos, G5333, 3 Revelation occurrences) carry both drug-mixing and sorcery senses, and context does not isolate one. Confidence is medium because the verdict is reached by convergence of multiple word groups rather than by any single lemma (dictionary headword) naming a modern recreational drug category.

scripture.force: 'Drug-mixing or sorcery' (pharmakeia) appears in the works-of-the-flesh catalog. The lemma (dictionary headword) denotes mixing and administering of drugs and potions and by extension sorcery practiced through such potions. Two canon occurrences only (here and Revelation 18:23), so its sense is not triangulated (pinned down by multiple lines of evidence) by frequency alone; placement among enumerated sins frames the practice negatively at the word-meaning level.

'Drunken bouts' (methai, plural of methe) and 'revels' (komoi, plural of komos) close the vice list, and the apodosis (the 'then' clause of an if-then statement) 'that those who practice such things will not inherit the kingdom of God' (hoti hoi ta toiauta prassontes basileian theou ou kleronomesousin) states the consequence. The future indicative (a simple statement about what will happen) plus accusative (the direct object grammatical form) encodes exclusion as the result, marking intoxication-aimed behavior as kingdom-disqualifying conduct.

'Do not be made drunk with wine' (me methyskesthe oino) is a present middle/passive imperative (an ongoing command, either reflexive or 'don't let it happen to you') with negation, prohibiting the ongoing state of being made drunk on wine. The relative clause 'in which is reckless dissipation' (en ho estin asotia) labels that state as dissipation or reckless waste (asotia). The contrasting command is 'be filled with the Spirit' (plerousthe en pneumati). The grammatical target is the intoxicated condition itself, not the substance class, so the prohibition extends by word-meaning logic to any agent producing the same loss of governed faculties.

'Drunken bouts' (methai) and 'revels' (komoi) are paired again in Paul's exhortation to walk as in the day. The same word pair that closes the Galatians vice list reappears here, supplying a second epistolary (letter-genre) attestation that locks the negative valence (the loaded negative tone) of the intoxication vocabulary.

'Revels' (komoi) and 'drinking-bouts' (oinophlugiai) are grouped with 'lawless idolatries' (athemitois eidololatriais) as part of what the gentile life was characterized by and what the believer is no longer to share. The juxtaposition (the deliberate side-by-side placement) encodes intoxication-aimed practice as part of a renounced past.

'Reckless dissipation' (asotia), the same lemma Ephesians 5:18 uses to label drunkenness, here describes the 'flood' (anachusin) of dissipation that outsiders are surprised believers no longer join. The second canonical use of asotia ties it directly to a lifestyle of intoxication-aimed excess.

'Drunkards' (methusoi, plural of methusos) sit in the catalog of those who will not inherit the kingdom of God, alongside revilers and the greedy. The agent noun (the noun form naming the person who does the action) names the person characterized by the intoxicated state, attaching kingdom-exclusion to the practice in a parallel structure to Galatians 5:21.

Jesus warns the disciples not to let their hearts be weighed down by 'dissipation or surfeiting' (kraipale), 'drunkenness' (methe), and the cares of life so that the day come on them suddenly. The word 'drunkenness' (methe) appears in a dominical saying (a saying of the Lord Jesus), broadening the word-pattern beyond Pauline letter catalogs.

'Be sober' (nepsate, from nepho) is an aorist imperative (a command for a single, complete action) paired with 'be watchful' (gregoresate) against the adversary. The verb 'be sober' (nepho) denotes a clear, unintoxicated, alert mental state. The command makes sobriety a standing obligation, so deliberate self-intoxication stands as its word-meaning opposite.

'Let us be sober' (nephomen, from nepho) sets sobriety against sleep and drunkenness in verses 6 to 8, where being drunk is associated with night and sobriety with day and with the armor of faith and love. The metaphor of day and night runs alongside a literal word-meaning contrast of 'be sober' (nepho) with intoxication.

'Be sound-minded and sober for prayers' (sophronesate kai nepsate eis proseuchas) pairs the two sobriety verbs in a single imperative chain. 'Be sound-minded' (sophroneo) denotes sound, governed mental faculties; 'be sober' (nepho) denotes the unintoxicated state. The combination strengthens the sobriety norm by joining cognitive composure to non-intoxication.

'Sober, temperate' (nephalious, from nephalios) heads the qualifications for older men. The adjective is cognate (from the same root) with 'be sober' (nepho) and designates the temperate condition as a standing virtue of mature believers, reinforcing the sobriety norm at the level of stable character.

'Self-control' (egkrateia) closes the fruit of the Spirit list. The noun denotes mastery over appetite and impulse. As Spirit-produced fruit it stands in direct word-meaning tension with the surrender of self-governance that intoxication-aimed substance use seeks.

'Self-control' (egkrateia) appears in the Petrine virtue chain between 'knowledge' (gnosis) and 'endurance' (hupomone). The second canonical use of the noun confirms its function as a standing Christian virtue rather than a one-off coinage, reinforcing the self-governance norm.

The 'body' (soma) is named the 'temple' (naos) of the Holy Spirit, and the clause 'you are not your own' (ouk este heauton) states that believers are not their own. This grounds bodily conduct in stewardship rather than autonomy, supplying the basis for treating self-harming intoxication as illegitimate use of a body that belongs to God.

'Therefore glorify God in your body' (doxasate de ton theon en to somati hymon) is an aorist imperative (a command for a complete action) grounded in the preceding clause about being bought with a price. The command sets a positive criterion for bodily conduct that deliberate intoxication does not meet.

'Let every person be subject to the governing authorities' (pasa psyche exousiais hyperechousais hypotassestho) establishes that the authorities are 'appointed' (tetagmenai) by God. This supplies the word-meaning hinge for the lawbreaking clause of the proposition, where illegal drugs engage civil ordinance.

'The one resisting the authority' (ho antitassomenos te exousia) is said to resist 'the ordinance of God' (te tou theou diatage), and such resisters will receive 'judgment' (krima) to themselves. The clause attaches a judgment consequence to defying lawful authority, which couples with the illegal aspect of the practice in view.

'Wine' (yayin) is called 'a mocker' (lets) and 'strong drink' (shekar) 'a brawler' (homeh), and the verse concludes that whoever staggers by them is not wise. The wisdom-genre verdict on intoxication-aimed substance use is negative through personification (giving human traits to non-human things) of the substances as agents of folly.

'Woe' (hoy) opens against those who rise early to pursue 'strong drink' (shekar) and tarry late till 'wine' (yayin) inflames them. The prophetic woe-oracle (a formal pronouncement of doom) attaches divine judgment to the lifestyle of intoxication-pursuit, supplying the same loaded negative tone the New Testament vice lists carry.

'Woe' (hoy) is pronounced on the one who gives his neighbor drink, joining his wrath, even 'making him drunk' (shakar), in order to look on their nakedness. The prophetic curse attaches woe to deliberately inducing intoxication in another, the closest Old Testament analog to administering an incapacitating substance.

'Wine' (yayin) and 'strong drink' (shekar) are prohibited to Aaron and his sons when entering the tent of meeting, on pain of death, so they may distinguish between holy and common. The Torah-genre (the legal books of Moses) restriction explicitly attaches faculties for discernment to the unintoxicated state, supplying the Pentateuchal (from the first five books) anchor for the sober-mindedness norm.

'Drug-practices or sorceries' (pharmakon, genitive plural meaning 'of-the-drug-practices', from pharmakos or related noun form) appears in a list of unrepented sins alongside murders, fornication, and thefts. The apocalyptic (end-times revelation genre) catalog places the practice among acts from which the unrepentant did not turn, reinforcing the loaded negative tone, although the sorcery sense is also attested.

'The drug-practicers or sorcerers' (pharmakois, dative plural of pharmakos) are listed among those whose portion is the lake of fire, sitting with murderers, the sexually immoral, and idolaters. The drug-mixing sense of the lemma (dictionary headword) carries severe judgment context, but the term also reaches the sorcery sense in apocalyptic usage, so the verse complicates the verdict by word-meaning underdetermination (where one word covers more than one meaning and context doesn't pin it down).

'Drug-practicers or sorcerers' (pharmakoi, plural of pharmakos) are again listed outside the new Jerusalem with dogs, the sexually immoral, murderers, idolaters, and everyone who loves and practices falsehood. The third 'drug-mixer or sorcerer' (pharmakos) occurrence sits in a similar exclusion catalog, but the same sorcery/drug-mixing ambiguity persists and the verse does not isolate recreational intoxication by itself.

complicating_texts.resolution: Paul tells Timothy to 'use a little wine' (oino oligo chro) for his stomach and frequent ailments. This permits a measured, medicinal use of a substance and shows the word-meaning target is not substance contact in itself but the intoxicated state. The proposition concerns intoxication-aimed use, so a medicinal small-quantity directive does not contradict it.

'Drug-mixer or sorcerer' (pharmakos) in Revelation carries both the sorcery sense and the drug-mixing sense, and the context (lists of unrepented sins) does not by word-meaning isolate one over the other. The word is retained as supporting because the word group fuses potion-making with the practice in the Greco-Roman setting, but the semantic breadth (the wide range of senses one word can hold) is the reason verdict confidence is held at medium and 'drug-mixer or sorcerer' (pharmakos) is not treated as a single decisive proof.

The psalm speaks of wine that gladdens the human heart as a gift within creation. This affirms moderate enjoyment of a created substance, not intoxication. It complicates a blanket ban on any psychoactive substance but does not bear against the narrower proposition about intoxication-aimed and illegal use, which the sobriety and self-control lemmas (dictionary headwords) oppose.

Jesus produces 'good wine' (oinos kalos) at Cana and the master of the feast says people serve poorer wine when guests 'have become drunk' (methysthosin, from methysko). The narrative attests legitimate festal use of wine but the verb 'make drunk' (methysko) in verse 10 is descriptive of guest behavior at feasts, not endorsed practice. The episode does not by word-meaning license intoxication.

The Nazirite vow abstains from 'wine' (yayin) and 'strong drink' (shekar) as a special consecration. By itself the law makes intoxicating drink permitted to the non-vowed and forbidden to the vowed, which complicates any universal substance ban. It is not closed within the lexical (word-meaning based) store alone because the Nazirite category is voluntary and does not generalize, but the unaddressed remainder is the scope question: the words restrict only Nazirites, not all Israel, so they leave open whether the general intoxication prohibition emerges from another word group rather than from this law.

variants.note: The cited verses lie outside the 3 John CBGM (Coherence-Based Genealogical Method, a statistical method for tracing manuscript families) published sample. No variant unit in the bundle touches the anchor lemmas (key dictionary headwords) 'drunkenness' (methe), 'revelry' (komos), 'reckless dissipation' (asotia), 'drug-mixing or sorcery' (pharmakeia), 'drug-mixer or sorcerer' (pharmakos), 'be sober' (nepho), 'self-control' (egkrateia), 'be drunk' (shakar), 'drunkard' (shikkor), 'strong drink' (shekar), 'wine' (yayin), or 'judgment' (krima) in a way that would alter the verdict, so the reading is treated as variant robust under ecm-shadow status (running in shadow against the critical edition of New Testament textual variants without yet being treated as authoritative).

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads the convergence of 'drunkenness' (methe), 'be made drunk' (methysko), 'drunkard' (methusos), 'revelry' (komos), 'reckless dissipation' (asotia), 'drinking-bouts' (oinophlugia) in vice lists, plus the positive 'be sober' (nepho), 'be sound-minded' (sophroneo), 'temperate' (nephalios), 'self-control' (egkrateia) word group, plus the Old Testament 'be drunk' (shakar) and 'drunkard' (shikkor) woe oracles, as a pan-canonical (spread across the whole Bible) word-pattern condemning the intoxicated state regardless of the substance employed, and treats recreational drug use as a contemporary instance of the same word-meaning category.

Notes that no canonical lemma (dictionary headword in the Bible) names cannabis, opiates, or any modern recreational drug category, that 'drug-mixing or sorcery' (pharmakeia) and 'drug-mixer or sorcerer' (pharmakos) carry an attested sorcery sense that context does not exclude, and that the prohibition therefore reaches recreational drugs only by inference from the intoxication-state vocabulary rather than by direct naming. On this reading the verdict is best stated as a principled inference rather than a direct word-meaning naming.

Reads the pharmak- group as primarily drug-mixing in its lexical root (the basic word-stem from which related words are formed) and treats the sorcery sense as historically derivative of potion-making practice, so that 'drug-mixing or sorcery' (pharmakeia) and 'drug-mixer or sorcerer' (pharmakos) in Galatians 5:20, Revelation 9:21, 18:23, 21:8, and 22:15 are taken as directly naming substance-induced altered states alongside the sorcery practiced through them.

hermeneutics.notes: The verdict rests on the analogy of Scripture (the principle that clearer texts interpret less clear ones across the canon). The named lemmas (key dictionary headwords) condemn the intoxicated state ('be drunk' (shakar), 'drunkard' (shikkor), 'drunkenness' (methe), 'be made drunk' (methysko), 'drunkard' (methusos), 'reckless dissipation' (asotia), 'revelry' (komos), 'drinking-bouts' (oinophlugia)) and command its opposite ('be sober' (nepho), 'be sound-minded' (sophroneo), 'temperate' (nephalios), 'self-control' (egkrateia)), and Romans 13 supplies the law-and-judgment vocabulary that engages the illegal-drug clause. The proposition is reached by joining these strands rather than by a single verse that names modern recreational drug categories.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: How does the lexical (word-meaning) pattern treat deliberate intoxication through ingested substances, and does it attach the vocabulary of sin or lawbreaking to such use?
stem_audit.notes: The original stem fuses an ethical category (sin) and a civil category (lawbreaking) and presupposes a settled negative verdict on recreational drug use. The neutral rephrasing asks what the word-pattern attaches to deliberate intoxication without asserting the conclusion. The verdict is still derived on the original stem, and the lexical (word-meaning based) evidence supports it on the intoxication and submission-to-authority strands while leaving the modern substance taxonomy itself unnamed by any lemma (dictionary headword). Direct queries of the lexical graph corrected the prior 'drug-mixing or sorcery' (pharmakeia, G5331) occurrence count from 3 to 2 and split out 'drug-mixer or sorcerer' (pharmakos, G5333) as a distinct lemma occurring 3 times (Revelation 9:21, 21:8, 22:15).

lay_summary: Several Greek and Hebrew word groups bear on this question, even though no single verse names modern recreational drugs by class. In Galatians 5:20-21, 'drug-mixing or sorcery' (pharmakeia), a word for mixing and administering drugs and potions, appears in a list of the works of the flesh next to 'drunken bouts' (methe) and 'revels' (komos), and the passage says those who practice such things will not inherit the kingdom of God. Ephesians 5:18 gives a direct command 'do not be drunk on wine' and calls that state 'reckless dissipation' (asotia). Romans 13:13, First Peter 4:3-4, and First Corinthians 6:10 carry the same vice vocabulary, attaching kingdom-exclusion to 'the drunkard' (methusos). On the positive side, the verbs 'be sober' (nepho) and 'be sound-minded' (sophroneo) and the adjective 'temperate' (nephalios) are commanded across First Peter 5:8, First Thessalonians 5:6-8, First Peter 4:7, Titus 2:2, and Second Timothy 4:5, and 'self-control' (egkrateia) is named as fruit of the Spirit in Galatians 5:23 and as a Christian virtue in Second Peter 1:6. Together these words set up a clear norm of governed, alert faculties, and intoxication-aimed substance use is the direct opposite of that norm. The Hebrew Bible already carries the same weight: 'be drunk' (shakar) and 'drunkard' (shikkor) with 'strong drink' (shekar) and 'wine' (yayin) appear in woe oracles in Isaiah 5:11,22, in Habakkuk 2:15 against the one who gives a neighbor drink to incapacitate him, in Proverbs 20:1 and 23:29-35, and in the priestly restriction of Leviticus 10:9. The lawbreaking part of the question connects to Romans 13:1-2, where every person is told to be subject to the governing authorities and the one who resists incurs 'judgment' (krima). First Corinthians 6:19-20 adds that the body is the temple of the Holy Spirit and that believers are to glorify God in the body. The point of confusion is that 'drug-mixing or sorcery' (pharmakeia) and 'drug-mixer or sorcerer' (pharmakos) can also mean sorcery, so they do not by themselves isolate recreational drug use, and texts like First Timothy 5:23 and Psalm 104:15 permit measured, non-intoxicating use of wine. For that reason the word-pattern supports the proposition through the convergence of the intoxication, sobriety, self-control, and submission word groups rather than through any one decisive term, and confidence is set at medium.
